subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: rescheduling with friends by phone [Action]
passage: Rain had washed out the Saturday street fair in Guadalajara, and Javier stood at the window with his shoes already on. He could sulk. Instead he picked up the phone in the hall and called his friend Mateo. "Fair is off today. Same fair next Sunday at two?" Mateo said yes. Then Javier called Rosa. "Sunday at two, at the corner by the bakery," he said, and Rosa laughed. "I will bring my brother's kite for after." Javier wrote SUNDAY 2:00 on a sticky note and pressed it on the fridge. One more call, to Diego, and they were four. The letdown felt smaller already.

qa.q: What time and place did Javier suggest for the new plan?
qa.a: He suggested Sunday at two, at the corner by the bakery.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling as he stood at the window, and what did he do about it?
qa.a: Disappointed, since his shoes were already on, but he chose to make calls instead of sulking. 😔

qa.q: What could Javier do if one friend cannot make Sunday?
qa.a: He could offer another day or go with those who can and share what happened afterwards, because it keeps the plan alive.

qa.q: How might Rosa see Javier's quick call?
qa.a: As a welcome sign that the day was not lost, since Rosa laughed and offered to bring a kite.

grounding: After a rained-off outing a boy phones his friends and fixes the next Sunday before the excitement fades.

subtype: Approach: finishing homework first, then playing [Action]
passage: The games corner beside the hostel common room opened at five, but Yogesh made his own rule: homework first, even when the others were already at the screen. On Monday he sat through prep hour with his maths and Hindi while the shouting from the games corner drifted in. Tarun, the warden on duty, glanced at Yogesh's copy and said nothing. At half past five Yogesh closed the last notebook, zipped his bag and walked in. The first level felt different: no little voice at the back of his head saying "you have not finished." He laughed louder than usual, and even won. At lights-out his bag was already packed for the morning.

qa.q: At what time did the games corner open?
qa.a: The games corner opened at five.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when he finally started the game, and why?
qa.a: Light and relaxed, because the homework was finished and nothing nagged at the back of his head, so he laughed louder than usual.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do if his homework takes longer than the prep hour?
qa.a: He could split the work and finish the rest before bed or ask for help, because the rule of work first still holds.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Yogesh's rule?
qa.a: As a sign of self-discipline, since Tarun glanced at the copy and said nothing, which suggests there was nothing to correct.

grounding: A boy in a hostel makes a rule that games start after homework and finds the game more enjoyable with the work done.

passage: Seema set the kitchen timer for forty minutes and pressed the button before opening her game. Weekday rule, her own: forty minutes, no more. Halfway through a tricky level her younger brother Kamal hovered, waiting for his turn on the shared tablet. With five minutes left she was one move from a treasure chest. The timer rang. Seema's thumb froze. "Just--" she began, then stopped, saved her place and handed Kamal the tablet. "Papa did not tell me to," she said, half proud, half cross. "I did." Kamal blinked. "You never stop." "Now I do." Tomorrow the treasure chest would be waiting.

qa.q: How long did Seema set the timer for?
qa.a: She set the timer for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when the timer rang one move from the chest?
qa.a: Torn, half proud and half cross, since her thumb froze but she stopped anyway. 😅

qa.q: What could Seema do if the timer often rings at a bad moment in a game?
qa.a: She could choose a game or level with natural stopping points, because the limit then holds without cutting the fun short.

qa.q: How might Kamal see Seema stopping on her own?
qa.a: With surprise and probably relief, since he blinked, said she never stops, and now gets his turn.

grounding: A girl sets a forty-minute timer for weekday games and stops when it rings, so the limit feels like her own rule.

passage: Abhinav sat down at seven with the tablet, telling himself: one round, then maths. The round ended in a narrow loss, so one more. Then a new level unlocked, and it would be silly to leave it. Mummy called him for dinner; he ate quickly and came back. At nine he promised himself the last level. At ten past ten the screen dimmed with a low-battery buzz, and Abhinav looked at the clock, then at the maths worksheet, still white and empty. His eyes stung. He copied two sums badly and left the rest. Next morning the teacher's red pen went through nearly the whole page.

qa.q: At what time did the screen dim with the low-battery buzz?
qa.a: The screen dimmed at ten past ten.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he looked at the empty worksheet?
qa.a: Dismay and tiredness, since his eyes stung and he rushed two sums badly.

qa.q: What approach could keep a game from taking over the evening?
qa.a: Decide a stopping point before starting, such as a timer or a set number of rounds, because "one more" has no end otherwise.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's teacher see the worksheet the next morning?
qa.a: As a sign that the homework was not really tried, since a red pen went through nearly the whole page, and the teacher may ask what happened.

grounding: A child keeps saying one more round until it is ten at night with the maths unfinished.

subtype: Approach: weighing what matters more this week [Thinking]
passage: Lalit's friends were online at six, and the new level was calling. But Friday was the science test. He looked at the two things side by side. Games will be there on Saturday, he thought. The test will not wait. Which one is due soon, and which can wait? He typed one line to his friend Om: "Studying till Friday. Saturday for sure." Then he took out his notes. Irawati, his mother, looked in and found him copying a diagram, lips moving. "No game tonight?" "Not till the weekend," Lalit said. "It will still be there." She left the door open and a cup of tea on the desk.

qa.q: Which test did Lalit have on Friday?
qa.a: Lalit had the science test on Friday.

qa.q: What was Lalit thinking when he weighed the game against the test?
qa.a: He felt the pull of the game but reasoned that the test was urgent while the game could wait until Saturday.

qa.q: What other approach could help Lalit keep to this choice?
qa.a: He could make a short study plan for each evening and put the game device away, because a fixed plan with no temptation nearby makes the choice easier.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Lalit's decision?
qa.a: Proudly and a little surprised, since she found him copying a diagram and left tea on the desk, which suggests she supports the choice.

grounding: A boy with a Friday test decides studying is urgent now and games can wait for the weekend.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a fair deal with parents [Action]
passage: Note, Monday. I am Pradeep and I look after Farida after school. On Saturday evening I was at her house when she asked her parents to sit down and laid out a plan on paper: weekdays for homework and reading as usual, and an hour of play on both weekend days. Her father asked how they would know she kept the study plan. Farida offered to show her planner every Sunday night. Her mother said, "Let us see how the next four weeks go, then talk." Farida shook both their hands, grinning, and I suggested she copy the agreement neatly and stick it near her desk. She did that straight away.

qa.q: How much gaming time did Farida ask for on the weekend?
qa.a: She asked for an hour of play on both weekend days.

qa.q: How did Farida feel as her parents agreed?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased, since she shook both their hands, grinning. 😊

qa.q: What could Farida do if she misses her study plan one week?
qa.a: Tell her parents plainly and repeat the week with a fix, because the deal depends on trust.

qa.q: How might Farida's parents see the plan?
qa.a: As a fair trial, since her mother said to see how four weeks go, and the planner gives them a way to check.

grounding: A girl offers weekend gaming hours in return for keeping her weekday study plan, and her parents agree to try it.

subtype: Approach: hiding the game and lying about homework [Pitfall]
passage: I am Aadhya, and I share a room with my brother Vihaan, so I saw it all. On Monday Vihaan told Mummy, "Homework is finished," and then took the game under his blanket with the sound turned low. He did it on Tuesday and Wednesday too. On Thursday, Alka Ma'am wrote in his diary that two assignments were missing. Mummy read the note twice. Vihaan's ears went red and he looked at the floor. "It is not only the marks," Mummy said quietly. "You told me it was done." The console went into the cupboard in her room for the week. Vihaan said nothing to me that night, and I could not tell if he was sorry or just cross.

qa.q: What did Alka Ma'am write in Vihaan's diary?
qa.a: She wrote that two assignments were missing.

qa.q: What might Vihaan have been feeling when Mummy read the note?
qa.a: Ashamed and worried, since his ears went red and he looked at the floor, though Aadhya cannot tell if he was sorry or just cross.

qa.q: What could Vihaan do to begin rebuilding Mummy's trust?
qa.a: Tell the truth about how much homework is left, finish the missing work and show it to her each evening, because steady honesty rebuilds trust.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about Vihaan's words on Monday?
qa.a: Hurt and disappointed, since she said it was not only the marks and that he had told her the work was done.

grounding: A boy claims homework is done and plays in secret, and the teacher's note brings both a marks problem and lost trust.

subtype: Approach: using the game as a reward for goals [Thinking]
passage: Sumit, put that tablet down a moment. Let me tell you how I thought at your age. I am Hansa, and at ten I had a little handheld game with a tiny screen that I adored. Homework and the game fought for every evening, and the game usually won. One night I thought: the game is not my enemy, it can be my prize. So I made a rule and said it aloud to Amma: "Two chapters first, then thirty minutes of my game." I put the game on the top shelf, turned the clock to face me, and read fast. I remember finishing the second chapter and feeling my heart hop. Thirty minutes felt sweeter than the whole afternoon used to.

qa.q: What was Hansa's rule for earning the game?
qa.a: Hansa's rule was two chapters first, then thirty minutes of the game.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling at the end of the second chapter?
qa.a: Excited and pleased, since Hansa's heart hopped at the thought of the reward.

qa.q: What other approach could Hansa use if two chapters felt too big?
qa.a: Split the goal into smaller steps, such as one chapter and ten minutes of play, because a reachable goal is easier to keep.

qa.q: How might Hansa's mother see the new rule?
qa.a: Probably with relief that Hansa made a plan alone, since Hansa said it aloud to Amma and the game stopped competing with the book.

grounding: A child turns the game into a reward after two chapters, so it motivates rather than competes with study.

subtype: Approach: noticing tiredness and changing the routine [Revision]
passage: The school bus came at 6:40, and Anand had been getting into bed after midnight because of the game. On Tuesday his head dropped in Sharmila Ma'am's class, and he jerked awake to laughter and a page of blank notes. That stung. On the bus home he added it up: sleep lost, notes lost, and he had not even won. By afternoon he had a new plan. He would play from four to five, right after snack, and the console would go into the hall cupboard at nine, before brushing his teeth. The next Tuesday he was awake for the whole lesson and even asked a question.

qa.q: At what time did Anand decide the console would go into the cupboard?
qa.a: He decided it would go in at nine, before brushing his teeth.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he woke up to the laughter in class?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since his head dropped and he woke to laughter and a page of blank notes.

qa.q: What else could help Anand besides moving the game?
qa.a: He could keep a fixed bedtime and wind down with a book, because a steady routine helps him wake up ready for the early bus.

qa.q: How might Sharmila Ma'am see Anand's change?
qa.a: With pleasure and some surprise, since he was awake for the whole lesson and even asked a question.

grounding: After falling asleep in class from late gaming, a boy sees the cost and moves the game to the afternoon.

subtype: Approach: playing a game with friends instead of alone [Thinking]
passage: Mei noticed that the pull was strongest when she was alone: with nobody around, one round became three hours and the afternoon vanished. So she made a plan. On Saturdays her cousins Freya and Noah came to her flat in Auckland, and that was when the console came out, all three of them shouting at the screen. On other days it stayed in its box. On Wednesday Mei missed it and stared at the box for a while. Then she took her bike out instead. By Saturday the game felt better than ever: Freya laughed so hard at Mei's crash that she fell off the sofa. When the cousins left, playing simply stopped.

qa.q: On which day did Mei's cousins come over?
qa.a: Mei's cousins came over on Saturdays.

qa.q: How did Mei feel on Wednesday when she stared at the box?
qa.a: She missed the game and felt the pull, but she chose to go cycling instead.

qa.q: What could Mei do if the cousins cannot visit for a few weeks?
qa.a: Play with a friend on a video call for a set time or plan another shared activity, because company is what keeps the game limited and fun.

qa.q: How might Freya see the Saturday game sessions?
qa.a: As great fun, since Freya laughed so hard at Mei's crash that she fell off the sofa.

grounding: A girl finds solo play hard to stop, so she plays only when her cousins are around, which limits time and adds fun.
